narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 76.7% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because the law school sets a high bar for admission, this probability led to your application being rejected.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors from your academic record. Your class ranking at the end of your third year was the strongest influence, pushing the prediction strongly toward failure. Your first-year ranking also worked against you, though with less force. Your undergraduate GPA was the only factor that pulled slightly in the positive direction, but it was not nearly enough to offset the other two.

Compared with students who were accepted, you finished both your first and third years in the bottom decile of your class, while successful applicants averaged around the middle of the pack (roughly 6th decile). Your LSAT score of 28 and undergraduate GPA of 2.90 were also noticeably below the averages of 37 and 3.23 seen among admitted students. Your middle family income, gender, and race played no role in the model’s decision.

To improve your chances, focus on strengthening your academic performance and consider retaking the LSAT to raise your score. Building a stronger record in these areas will directly address the factors that weighed most heavily against you. (218 words)
